title: Three vows (ch. 58)

lines: THE RULE READ TO HIM, AGAIN.
IF YOU CAN KEEP IT, COME IN.
cards: Don't make it easy to get in. That's roughly how chapter fifty-eight of Saint Benedict's Rule greets newcomers who ask to join.
The one who asks is left waiting, and has to put up with a little rudeness at the door, to see if he means it. If he keeps asking, he's let in, first to the guest house, then to the novices.
The Rule itself is read aloud to him, more than once: this is the law you want to serve under. If you can keep it, come in. If not, you are free to go.
Today, the promise he makes at the end of all that.

teach.b: When the time comes, the novice stands before the whole community in the oratory, the place of prayer, and promises three things: stability, conversion of life, and obedience. Obedience had its own day earlier.
Today is the first one, stability: binding yourself to one community, in one place, for life. A monk doesn't go looking for a better monastery when this one gets hard.

He stays with these brothers, this abbot, this kitchen, this choir. In the Rule's first chapter, Benedict has sharp words for monks who wander from house to house. Stability is his answer to that restlessness.
Conversion of life is harder to pin down. The Latin phrase is unusual, and readers argue over its exact sense.

teach.h: THE PROMISE LAID ON THE ALTAR.
teach.b: Some hear a promise to live the monastic way of life; others, a promise to keep being changed, day after day. The novice writes his promise out, in his own hand if he can, and lays it on the altar himself.

teach.h: UPHOLD ME ACCORDING TO THY WORD, AND I SHALL LIVE.
teach.b: He sings a verse from the psalms, in the Douay-Rheims: "Uphold me according to thy word, and I shall live: and let me not be confounded in my expectation." The community sings it back to him.
Then he lies at each brother's feet and asks for their prayers, and from that day, the Rule says, he's counted one of them.

teach.h: THE FIRST VOW IS NOT LEAVING.
teach.b: The first vow isn't about doing anything grand. It's about not leaving. The holiness Benedict has in mind grows in one patch of ground, among the same faces.

how: Benedictine monks and nuns make their vows of stability, conversion of life and obedience during Mass or in the community's church, and the written promise is placed on the altar, as the Rule describes.

o: a promise to keep the same schedule every day
a monk's promise to stay with one community for life
a calm, steady mood kept up through daily prayer

p: if you can keep it, come in

s: in the Rule, a newcomer is welcomed in at once
chapter fifty-eight says entry should not be made easy. he's left waiting first.
stability means staying with one community
the monk binds himself to these brothers in this place, and doesn't go looking for a better house.
everyone agrees what conversion of life means
the Latin phrase is unusual, and readers argue over its exact sense.

games.q: you've waited at the door, lived as a novice, and heard the Rule read to you. now you're told: if you can keep it, come in; if not, you are free to go. what happens next in chapter fifty-eight?
o: a quiet handshake with the abbot, and you're in.
you write your promise, lay it on the altar, and sing a psalm verse.
you take a new name and leave for another house.
games.why: the novice writes his promise, lays it on the altar himself, and sings "uphold me according to thy word"; the community sings it back.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you've already said yes to, a person, a job, a promise, a place, and notice whether part of you has been edging toward the door. Don't fix it; just name it, and for these two minutes, stay.
If you pray, say the psalm line slowly: uphold me according to thy word.

wordCard.voice: Stability. The first of the three promises in Benedict's Rule: binding yourself to one community and one place, and staying. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, the first of the three promises in chapter fifty-eight of the Rule.

carryVoice: Your line: stay. Of Benedict's three promises, it's the first and the plainest. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Psalm 118:116 (Douay numbering; Psalm 119:116 in Hebrew numbering)
